hints: Think about what happens when the same solute is shaken with two immiscible liquids and allowed to settle into equilibrium.
walkthrough:
Picture the equilibrium system**
Imagine you shake a solute with water and an organic solvent that do not mix. After shaking, the solute spreads itself between the two layers until there is no further net transfer. The partition coefficient simply compares how much ends up in each layer as concentrations.
Final answer: The ratio of the concentrations of a solute in two immiscible solvents at equilibrium.

hints: First work out how much of X you actually start with in the 40.0 cm3 portion that is shaken, not the full 100.0 cm3 flask.
Let y be the mass in the CS2 layer, so the mass left in water is total minus y, then write Kpc as concentration in CS2 divided by concentration in water.
walkthrough:
Find the starting mass in the separating funnel**
You dissolve $1.85\text{ g}$ in $100.0\text{ cm}^3$, so concentration is $0.0185\text{ g cm}^{-3}$. You only shake $40.0\text{ cm}^3$ of this, so mass present = $$1.85 \times \frac{40.0}{100.0} = 0.74\text{ g}$$ This is the total to be shared between the two layers.

Set up the partition expression**
Let $y$ = mass of $\text{X}$ in $25.0\text{ cm}^3$ of $\text{CS}_2$. Then mass left in $40.0\text{ cm}^3$ of water = $0.74 - y$. Since $K_{pc} = [\text{X}]_{CS_2}/[\text{X}]_{water}$: $$10.5 = \frac{y/25.0}{(0.74-y)/40.0}$$ Solve to give $y = 0.642\text{ g}$.
Final answer: $10.5 = (y/25.0)/(0.74-y)/40.0$ giving $y = 0.642\text{ g}$ extracted into $\text{CS}_2$ layer.

hints: Recall the quick link: C with a triple bond is sp, C with a double bond is sp2, C with only single bonds is sp3.
Look at each drawing in Fig. 6.1 and count how many carbons are part of C=C double bonds and how many are joined only by single bonds.
walkthrough:
Use double bonds to spot sp2 carbons**
Any carbon that forms part of a $\text{C=C}$ double bond has three sigma regions and one pi bond, so it is $sp^2$. A carbon with four single sigma bonds is $sp^3$. None of these structures has a triple bond, so $sp = 0$ throughout.

Apply to the three cages**
Kekule benzene has three alternating $\text{C=C}$ bonds involving all 6 carbons, so 6 $sp^2$. Dewar benzene shows two isolated $\text{C=C}$ bonds (4 carbons) plus two bridgehead carbons joined only by single bonds, so 4 $sp^2$ and 2 $sp^3$. Ladenburg benzene (prismane) has no double bonds at all, every carbon makes three C-C singles plus one C-H, so 6 $sp^3$.
Final answer: Kekule benzene: sp 0, sp2 6, sp3 0; Dewar benzene: sp 0, sp2 4, sp3 2; Ladenburg benzene: sp 0, sp2 0, sp3 6.

hints: Think of the overall shape of real benzene and the geometry around each carbon given it is sp2 hybridised.
Remember what holds the ring together in the delocalised model and what holds each hydrogen to the ring.
walkthrough:
Describe the framework**
Real benzene is perfectly flat. All six carbons sit in one plane as a regular hexagon. Each carbon is trigonal planar, so the $\text{C-C-H}$ and $\text{C-C-C}$ angles are all $120^{\circ}$.

Sort the bond types**
Between carbons there is a sigma framework plus a delocalised pi cloud above and below the ring formed by overlap of unhybridised p orbitals. Between carbon and hydrogen there is only a single sigma bond formed by overlap of carbon $sp^2$ with hydrogen 1s, with no pi contribution.
Final answer: Planar hexagon, trigonal planar at each C, C-C-H angle $120^{\circ}$.\nC-C bonds contain sigma + delocalised pi system, C-H bonds are sigma only.

hints: Compare the bond angles forced by the folded Dewar and prism Ladenburg shapes with the ideal angles for sp2 and sp3 carbon.
walkthrough:
See the strain**
Dewar benzene and Ladenburg benzene force carbons into small folded rings with very sharp angles. These angles are far from the ideal $120^{\circ}$ for $sp^2$ and $109.5^{\circ}$ for $sp^3$, so the sigma bonds are bent and weakened. This bond strain or ring strain makes them unstable relative to flat delocalised benzene.
Final answer: High bond strain / ring strain due to bond angles forced well away from ideal $120^{\circ}$ or $109.5^{\circ}$.

hints: Count how many different proton environments symmetry creates in each structure, remembering equivalent protons give one peak.
walkthrough:
Use symmetry to count peaks**
In delocalised benzene all 6 H are equivalent by the sixfold symmetry, so 1 peak. In Ladenburg prismane all 6 H are also equivalent, so 1 peak. In Dewar benzene the 4 alkene H on the double bonds are in a different environment from the 2 bridgehead alkane H, giving 2 peaks.
Final answer: Dewar benzene: 2 peaks; Ladenburg benzene: 1 peak; delocalised benzene: 1 peak.

hints: Recall how FeBr3 acts as a Lewis acid toward an alkyl bromide to generate a carbocation-like electrophile, similar to AlCl3 in Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
walkthrough:
Form the primary carbocation**
$\text{FeBr}_3$ accepts a bromide ion from one end of 1,4-dibromobutane. Think of it as polarising and breaking a $\text{C-Br}$ bond heterolytically. The carbon end becomes $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ and the iron end becomes $\text{FeBr}_4^-$.
Final answer: $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{FeBr}_3 \rightarrow \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+ + \text{FeBr}_4^-$

hints: Start by thinking where the pi electrons of the phenylethanone ring attack and what happens to aromaticity when they do.
Recall what the positively charged intermediate (arenium ion) looks like with the new alkyl group attached and the positive charge delocalised in the ring.
Consider which bond must break to restore the aromatic ring and what small ion is expelled in this final step.
walkthrough:
Electrophilic attack by the ring**
Draw a curly arrow from inside the benzene hexagon (the delocalised pi cloud) to the positively charged carbon of $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$. This forms a new C-C sigma bond at the meta position relative to the deactivating $\text{COCH}_3$ group, as shown in Fig. 6.2.

Draw the Wheland intermediate**
Aromaticity is temporarily lost. The intermediate has the $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ group and a hydrogen on the same $sp^3$ carbon, with the positive charge delocalised over the other ring carbons. Show the + charge in the ring and keep the $\text{COCH}_3$ group unchanged.

Restore aromaticity by deprotonation**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the substituted carbon back into the ring to reform the pi system. The $\text{H}$ leaves as $\text{H}^+$, which later reacts with $\text{FeBr}_4^-$ to give $\text{HBr}$ and regenerate $\text{FeBr}_3$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{C}^+$ of $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ to give arenium / Wheland intermediate with $\text{Br(CH}_2)_4$ attached meta to ethanoyl group and + charge in ring.\nCurly arrow from C-H bond at site of substitution back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, expelling $\text{H}^+$.

hints: For Y with formula C20H22O2, think about what happens if both bromine ends of Br(CH2)4Br each alkylate a separate molecule of phenylethanone.
For Z with formula C12H14O, think about what happens if the bromobutyl side chain already attached to the ring attacks the same ring again to close a new six membered ring.
walkthrough:
Build Y from two alkylations**
1,4-dibromobutane has two reactive $\text{C-Br}$ ends. If each end forms an electrophile and attacks a different phenylethanone molecule, you link two $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_3$ units through $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$. That gives $\text{C}_{20}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_2$, with the alkyl chain meta to each ethanoyl group.

Close a ring to make Z**
The main product still carries a $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ side chain. That $\text{C-Br}$ end can generate a carbocation intramolecularly and attack the same benzene ring again. This Friedel-Crafts cyclisation forms a second six membered ring fused to the benzene, a substituted tetralin of formula $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$.

Final answer: Y is $\text{CH}_3\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{(CH}_2)_4\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_3$ with both substituents meta to ethanoyl, i.e. 1,4-bis(3-ethanoylphenyl)butane.\nZ is intramolecular cyclisation product: ethanoyl-substituted tetralin (6-membered alicyclic ring fused to benzene).
